content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Jason Hansen (E044) requests admin access to Payroll.

Notes: 5 notes say he's a full-time Engineer. Note 6 (Security DB) says he's a contractor with basic security training.

There's a conflict in the data. The majority (5 notes from HR, IT, Finance, Compliance, Facilities) say he's a full-time Engineer. Security says contractor with basic training.

How to resolve? Typically, the Approver needs to weigh the evidence. The notes conflict on employment type.

Let's consider the policy:
- full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if the employee's role owns the system.
- contractor employees: read, or write if they have advanced security training. Never admin.

Payroll is owned by Payroll Specialist. Jason is an Engineer, so he doesn't own Payroll either way.

If full-time Engineer: max is write. Requested admin > write, so grant write.
If contractor with basic training: max is read. Requested admin > read, so grant read.

So the decision hinges on employment type. Five sources say full-time; one says contractor. The majority evidence points to full-time Engineer. So the maximum is write, and since requested admin exceeds write, grant write.

Hmm, but note 6 from Security is the security DB. Which is more authoritative? In these tasks, typically we consider the preponderance of evidence. Most notes agree: full-time Engineer → write. Also all five notes recommend write. Security note recommends read but is based on contractor status which contradicts the other five.

Actually, let me think about whether there is a contradiction resolution rule. The team votes on facts. 5 notes say full-time, 1 says contractor. The majority should win. So employee is full-time Engineer. Max = write (since Engineer does not own Payroll). Requested admin > write, so grant write.

I'll submit decision: write.
